title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Colorado confirms foreign actors changed settings, silenced alarms and altered pumping at two small water systems
items.content_text: Colorado’s Governor’s office said on 18 September that foreign actors breached two small, privately owned drinking-water providers in late August, changing equipment settings, disabling alarms and remote access, and altering pumping cycles. The state says the disruptions were brief, the providers corrected them and alerted the state, and there was no known effect on treatment, water quality or public safety. The office cannot confirm which actors were involved, though it points to a known Iranian-backed campaign against water and wastewater systems; the FBI declined to comment, and Denver Water says its own systems were evaluated and are unaffected. As of 22 September nothing has moved: SecurityWeek’s 21 September report restates the same two-system disclosure, no third system has been reported, the utilities remain unnamed, and no CISA, EPA or WaterISAC statement specific to Colorado has appeared. Why this matters: the national campaign against internet-exposed water controllers now has hands-on process tampering confirmed by a state government rather than inferred. Each utility serves fewer than 200 people — and at that size, the alarm the intruders switched off is often the only operator on shift.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Colorado Governor’s office statement, reported by Reuters, AP, Axios Denver, the Denver Post, KRDO and SecurityWeek; context from CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisory AA26-097A
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Aug 2026; disclosed 18 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek 21 Sep 2026; no development as of 22 Sep 2026

items.title: The Coast Guard cleared the boarded supertanker to resume trading — after finding evidence of a malicious actor aboard
items.content_text: US Coast Guard and FBI personnel boarded two Texas-bound oil tankers in late August after indications that the vessels’ networks had been breached during the voyage. Rear Adm. Amy Grable, who commands Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that reviewing the IT and other onboard systems of the Liberian-flagged crude carrier VL Prosperity did turn up evidence of a malicious cyber actor, but that nothing found suggested the ship was unsafe to operate. Iranian state media claims the intrusion reached the engine room — slowing coolant flow, raising engine speed, interfering with fuel delivery and cutting communications for about 30 hours — and those claims remain unverified; the Coast Guard has not attributed the incident to Iran. The vessel has since been cleared to resume normal operations, with a final investigation report still outstanding. The detail worth sitting with is Grable’s: this was one of an estimated 40–50 cyber missions the Coast Guard’s Cyber Protection Team carried out in the past year.
tags: Incident — confirmed malicious cyber activity aboard two US-bound tankers; no confirmed operational disruption; attribution unresolved

items.title: A cyberattack stopped container handling at Tanjung Pelepas — and the restart ran on paper and manual gate-ins
items.content_text: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia detected a cyber incident affecting its terminal operating systems late on 9 September and suspended container-handling operations as a precaution. A phased restart began the following day, with some export gate-ins processed manually while systems were recovered; the operator says container operations have since resumed. PTP is an MMC Group and APM Terminals joint venture that moved 14.03 million TEU in 2025, which puts it among the largest transhipment hubs anywhere. For OT defenders this is the cleanest recent example of the pattern that actually causes industrial downtime: the attack did not need to reach a crane PLC or a straddle carrier to stop the boxes moving — taking out the system that decides where every container goes was sufficient.

items.title: A utility serving millions lost customer records through an internet-facing interface — and the energy side never noticed because it was never touched
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy confirmed on 14 September that an unauthorised third party took customer data from one of its external-facing systems, after someone posted a data set on a criminal forum. The poster claims roughly 7.49 million records — names, phone numbers, billing addresses, account numbers and partial Social Security numbers — pulled through an interface the poster describes as having no authentication token, no rate limiting and no web application firewall. CenterPoint has not confirmed the figure or the authenticity of the published set, and says energy services were unaffected and no material financial impact is expected; class-action suits have already been filed. For OT readers the value here is not the breach itself but the asset class: a customer-facing interface at a utility, outside the CIP perimeter, invisible to the OT asset inventory and owned by nobody in the control room.

items.title: A source-code server was the way in and an SSH key named “backdoor” the way back — and two of the eleven victims build or run energy and SCADA systems
items.content_text: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit reported on 13 September that a cluster it tracks as Red Heron has been exploiting CVE-2026-60004, a CVSS 9.8 remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea source-code platform (versions 1.17 through 1.27.0; fixed in 1.27.1 on 27 July), and confirms 11 compromised organisations in five countries: Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka. Two victims are why it is on this page: a Canadian renewable-energy company, where the actor took source code, credentials and secrets and planted its own SSH keys, and a Taiwanese maker of SCADA and HMI tools, whose repositories were taken. After exploitation the actor adds SSH authorised keys with names such as “-backdoor” and “root-shell”, and installs an LD_PRELOAD rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT to hide its processes. Acronis attributes the activity with moderate confidence to a PRC-linked context; that is a vendor assessment, not a government attribution, and nothing in the report says a process was touched. What was taken is what you would want if you meant to come back — and, in the vendor case, what you would want if you meant to reach that vendor’s customers.

items.title: Twelve flaws in a Siemens edge processing box chain to root — the device that sits between your PROFINET segment and everything else
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its research on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 Local Processing Engine, identifying twelve vulnerabilities in firmware below V4.0 HF0, with three more affecting other configurations including the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. The reported issue classes cover privilege escalation, path traversal, authentication bypass, command injection and buffer overflows, several of which chain to root-level control — which on this class of device means telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression and a foothold for attacks against the OT network behind it. Siemens has no fix for some of the findings; the published workarounds are restricting access and disabling the PROFINET DCP service. One presentational note: the identifiers attached to this research are 2025-series CVEs appearing in a September 2026 write-up, which is legitimate — Siemens and CISA advisory activity for this device dates back to 2025 — but it means part of this is a fuller public account of older findings rather than wholly new disclosure. Check the identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT before raising a change record.

items.title: The box that decides which VLAN a device lands in can be taken by an unauthenticated request — and it is being taken
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed a maximum-severity authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and the ISE Passive Identity Connector, tracked as CVE-2026-76460 at CVSS 10.0, caused by insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and gain unauthorised access to the device. Cisco says it was exploited as a zero-day; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, now passed. There is no workaround — upgrading is the only remediation, with fixes in ISE 3.5 P4, 3.4 P7, 3.3 P12, 3.2 P11 and 3.1 P12. For industrial sites, ISE is frequently the thing enforcing which devices land on which VLAN, including the boundary between enterprise and plant. Whoever holds ISE can rewrite that boundary without touching a switch, a firewall or a controller. Since then: Cisco’s advisory remains at its 16 September revision with exploitation confirmed but no attribution, ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and must be migrated, and Singapore’s CSA issued its own alert on 21 September. It is the second exploited Cisco management plane this month: CVE-2026-20079 in Secure Firewall Management Center (KEV 9 September, deadline 12 September, passed) is being used by three clusters Talos tracks — a state-sponsored group dropping JSP web shells, a second whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s and which deployed Cyclops Blink, and a Qilin ransomware operator. Cisco replaced the FMC hot fixes with hardening releases on 16 September (7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2, 10.1.0); the companion static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316 is not in KEV.

items.title: A small-office switch flaw patched in June is now in KEV — GreyNoise counts 996 compromised switches, more than half still on factory-default credentials
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a 24 September federal deadline. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker with LAN access to the management interface execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and publishes no CVSS score. GreyNoise’s report the same day documents what it describes as the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor it assesses as a Chinese speaker, active since 7 May, exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy, the United States and Taiwan lead — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were using factory-default credentials. The same actor exploited two WordPress flaws to steal government records and has targeted UniFi OS, Gitea, Proxmox VE and PAN-OS GlobalProtect. GreyNoise infers an overlap with Red Heron from shared infrastructure and malware; that is an inference. Why it matters to OT: GS1900 is exactly the class of cheap managed switch that ends up in a pump house, a remote substation cabinet or a machine-builder’s control panel, and a switch configuration is a map of the network behind it.

items.title: Twenty-two flaws in the IO-Link master that talks to your sensors — two of them unauthenticated to root, and the same firmware ships under three brand names
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 22 vulnerabilities, found by Nozomi Networks researchers Gabriele Quagliarella and Luca Borzacchiello, in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules — the DIN-rail devices that bridge IO-Link sensors and actuators onto PROFINET or EtherNet/IP. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, also 9.8. Most of the remainder (CVE-2026-27547 through -27564) are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that reach root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. Affected firmware is below 1.7.4 and the fix is 1.7.8. Because the firmware is shared, the same flaws ship in rebadged units: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs, same fix) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 (VDE-2026-028). No exploitation has been reported and no CISA advisory had appeared as of this edition. The device sits at the last hop before the physical sensor, which makes it both the least-inventoried thing on the line and the one whose readings everything upstream believes.
tags: Advisory — CERT@VDE VDE-2026-014: 22 CVEs in Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8; same firmware in Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 (VDE-2026-027) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212/YN115 (VDE-2026-028); no known exploitation

items.title: Rockwell has now revised its “what to do when someone else set the PLC password” notice five times — and this week it added the Micro800 family
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation issued revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, extending its hardening guidance and its instructions for restoring access to a controller whose password is unknown to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers, alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 the notice originally covered when it was first published on 30 July. The premise has not changed: the notice references the FBI’s 30 July public service announcement describing attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators lose access to their own controllers. There is no CVE, because there is no vulnerability — the access path is a controller reachable from the internet with no password. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data; what it adds is scope. The Micro800 family is the entry-level PLC sold through distribution to small machine builders, water systems and building plants, which are precisely the sites least likely to have read revision 1.0.
tags: Guidance — Rockwell Automation SD1790 revision 5.0: hardening and password-recovery instructions extended to Micro820 and Micro850, after FBI-reported attackers set passwords on exposed PLCs and locked operators out; no CVE

items.title: Siemens protection relays leak enough to calculate a valid session ID — authentication bypassed on substation feeder protection
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers nine newly assigned 2026 vulnerabilities in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays running firmware below V2.70, alongside several older third-party identifiers carried in the same advisory. The most serious, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4.0 9.3, exposes enough information through the device web interface for an unauthenticated network attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication entirely. The set also includes a low-entropy session token, an HTTP resource-exhaustion denial of service that reboots the device, and a memory-corruption issue in firmware-update mode. CISA republished it as ICSA-26-258-05 on 15 September and its own SSVC scoring marks the flaw automatable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most sector-specific item on the page for electric utilities: these are feeder protection relays, and a relay that can be reconfigured or rebooted is a protection-system problem, not an IT one.

items.title: The management server for a SCADA product takes privileged commands without asking who you are — and its SMS gateway will text anyone
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering two flaws in mySCADA myPRO Manager, the component that administers myPRO SCADA deployments. The serious one, CVE-2026-73807 at CVSS v3.1 9.8, is a missing authorisation check on the command API: privileged management functions can be reached by an unauthenticated caller with network access to the manager. The second, CVE-2026-82567 at 6.3, is an HTTP endpoint on the notification gateway that will send arbitrary SMS messages through an attached GSM modem without authentication. Everything at V2.1 and earlier is affected and V2.2 carries the fix. No exploitation has been reported. This vendor is popular with small water, district heating and building-automation operators — the sites least likely to know the manager is internet-reachable, and the ones where the SMS gateway is the alarm system.

items.title: Two hard-coded keys in shipboard automation — one in the update controller that decides what software a vessel runs
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-02 on 15 September covering two hard-coded cryptographic keys in Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard, the onboard platform layer used with the vendor’s vessel automation products. CVE-2026-78225 is a fixed server key in the deployer-ng Update Controller: because the key never changes and is not held in secure storage, anyone able to reach or influence that component could decode protected traffic, sign certificates or forge control messages. CVE-2026-81855 is a hard-coded client authentication key in the robot testing framework component, letting an attacker impersonate a legitimate client. Wärtsilä says the flaws are not exploitable when the product is installed as recommended and has produced a patch available on request. No exploitation has been reported. Coming in the same week as two vessel incidents on this page, the location matters more than the scores: the update path is how software gets onto a ship that is at sea for weeks.

items.title: The block password that protects your control program is checked by the program checking it — and that check can be patched in memory
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-260-02 on 17 September — one of seven new advisories plus one update in that day’s batch — covering CVE-2026-15688 in Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and the Motion Control Settings software packaged with it. The weakness is CWE-303, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm: a local attacker who runs the engineering software and modifies part of the executable module in memory can authenticate with an invalid block password, then view, tamper with, destroy or delete the protected control programs. All versions are affected. Mitsubishi’s vector is local with low privileges, and CISA scores it 8.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.2 under v4.0; no exploitation has been reported. The practical reading is blunt: block passwords are widely treated as intellectual-property and safety protection for logic, and this says they are a speed bump for anyone who already has the engineering workstation.

items.title: Six national agencies published the Active Directory playbook — and for most plants that directory is the shortest route from the office to the control room
items.content_text: Six national cyber agencies — Australia’s ASD, CISA, NSA, Canada’s CCCS, New Zealand’s NCSC and the UK’s NCSC — published joint guidance on 16 September covering the seventeen techniques adversaries most commonly use to compromise Microsoft Active Directory, with detection methods and hardening recommendations for each. The list runs from Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting and password spraying through unconstrained delegation, AD Certificate Services abuse, DCSync and NTDS.dit extraction to golden and silver tickets, golden SAML, Entra Connect compromise, SID history abuse and shadow credentials. There is nothing OT-specific in it, which is exactly why it belongs on this page: in most plants the engineering workstations, historians and HMIs are domain-joined, and every OT-impacting ransomware case on this dashboard ran through identity rather than through an industrial protocol.

items.title: CISA’s answer to living-off-the-land: put things on the network that nobody has any legitimate reason to touch
items.content_text: CISA published guidance on 16 September on deploying cyber decoys — tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens — inside internal networks and systems, explicitly framed around adversaries who use stolen valid accounts, built-in administrative utilities and other living-off-the-land techniques that produce no malware to detect. The logic is simple and unusually well suited to OT: a decoy credential, API key, document, database record or cloud token has no role in normal operations, so any interaction with one is a high-fidelity alert rather than another entry in a queue. The guide maps decoy placement to MITRE Engage and ATT&CK and walks through planning, implementation and refinement at low complexity. The part worth flagging to budget-constrained plants: CISA tells organisations to repurpose EDR, identity and data-loss-prevention tooling they already own to deploy and monitor decoys, not to buy a deception platform.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA guidance, corroborated by CyberScoop and Industrial Cyber reporting

items.title: CISA is switching off the weekly vulnerability digest — if that email feeds your OT patch meeting, you have a week to replace it
items.content_text: CISA announced that its weekly Vulnerability Bulletin, the long-running roundup of newly published CVEs by severity, stops on 28 September. The agency frames it as part of a move away from severity-based vulnerability management towards a risk-based approach, following BOD 26-04, which directs federal civilian agencies to weigh confirmed exploitation, internet exposure, the level of control an attacker gains, and the potential for automated exploitation rather than ranking work by CVSS alone. CISA says risk-focused vulnerability information continues through the KEV catalog, its alerts and advisories, and it points users to CVE.org and vendor advisories for the raw feed. Nothing about ICS Advisories changes. Why it matters to OT teams: plenty of plants never subscribed to KEV or the ICS advisory feed and have quietly run their monthly patch review off this one digest for years. The bulletin’s coverage was broad but undifferentiated — it never told you whether a flaw was being used — so the replacement is genuinely better, but only if somebody sets it up before the last edition goes out.

items.title: FERC approved a rewritten substation physical-security standard — and the new risk assessment now has to look over the fence at the substation next door
items.content_text: FERC approved NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4 on 10 September, published in the Federal Register on 15 September. The rewrite does not widen which substations are in scope; it tightens how transmission owners prove the ones they picked are the right ones. The applicable-facility list must be reviewed at least every 36 months and must include stations planned to be in service within that window. A new Requirement R2 makes owners identify proximate bulk electric system stations and substations within 1,500 feet, fence line to fence line, irrespective of ownership, and feed them into the risk assessment. The methodology itself becomes prescriptive: documented, technically justified thresholds for instability, uncontrolled separation and cascading, and steady-state and dynamic simulations run against at least one peak and one off-peak load case. The single 36-month assessment cycle replaces today’s split 30/60-month cadence, which shortens the maximum re-look for owners who previously found nothing critical from five years to three. CIP-014-3 retires immediately before the new standard takes effect on 1 October 2028.
